item.title: Students still waiting for subsidised bus cards as Term 3 approaches
item.description: Students who have been waiting for government-funded bus cards for months could face further uncertainty as Term 3 approaches, with concerns raised in Parliament over delays in the National Transport Assistance Scheme. The issue was raised in Parliament today following a question to the Minister for Education, Aseri Radrodro, about how the Ministry plans to ensure government funded student cards a
item.content:encoded:
Students who have been waiting for government-funded bus cards for months could face further uncertainty as Term 3 approaches, with concerns raised in Parliament over delays in the National Transport Assistance Scheme.

The issue was raised in Parliament today following a question to the Minister for Education, Aseri Radrodro, about how the Ministry plans to ensure government funded student cards are topped up on time in the future.

Radrodro says that eligible students must apply for transport assistance through their schools before the beginning of each school year.

He says applications are then assessed and verified by school heads before being processed by the Ministry.

Radrodro says for existing students, blue bus cards are expected to be topped up automatically during Terms 2 and 3.

The Ministry says cards are topped up twice each term, covering Weeks 1 to 7 and Weeks 8 to 14.

The Minister says delays could result from incomplete applications or information not being submitted and verified within the required timeframe.

He asked Opposition MP Hem Chand to provide the Ministry with a list of affected students and their details so the cases could be investigated and processed.

The Minister also reminded students to keep their cards safe.

Students who lose or damage their cards must apply for a replacement through their school and have the replacement activated through the Ministry's FEMIS system.

Radrodro says the Government has allocated $54 million in the 2026–27 Budget for student transport assistance. The programme supports more than 70,000 students through blue bus cards and more than 44,000 st udents through Rural Service Licences.

With Term 3 approaching, the immediate concern remains whether students who have already applied but are still waiting for their cards will receive them in time to avoid fu rther transport costs for their families.

item.title: Koro youth still struggling with emotional trauma from Cyclone Winston
item.description: The ongoing impact of Tropical Cyclone Winston on communities in Lomaiviti, particularly Koro Island, which was severely affected by the cyclone in 2016, has left some young people experiencing emotional trauma and still struggling to share their experiences. This was highlighted by the Lomaiviti Youth Provincial Council General Secretary Wini Gaunavou during the three day Regional Conference of Y
item.content:encoded:
The ongoing impact of Tropical Cyclone Winston on communities in Lomaiviti, particularly Koro Island, which was severely affected by the cyclone in 2016, has left some young people experiencing emotional trauma and still struggling to share their experiences.

This was highlighted by the Lomaiviti Youth Provincial Council General Secretary Wini Gaunavou during the three day Regional Conference of Youth Oceania 2026 hosted by the Pacific Islands Forum.

Gaunavou stresses that there needs to be more grassroots engagement and capacity building to ensure communities, especially youths, understand climate change, have a stronger voice in addressing it, and can share the challenges they face.

Insert: more engagement needed kk 19th Aug

She says the Government also needs to do more to bring grassroots voices into climate discussions.

Looking ahead to COP, Gaunavou says she hopes to bring real stories from communities affected by climate change so the voices of those at the grassroots level can be heard internationally.

Meanwhile, Traziel Judah of the University of the South Pacific Lau Student Association says Pacific countries must work together and strengthen youth involvement in addressing the impacts of climate change, as it has become a major concern for Pacific communities, especially small island nations affected by rising sea levels.

Judah says some communities are already experiencing changes to their traditional way of life due to climate change, including changes in environmental patterns that have guided communities for generations.

He says there is a need for Pacific nations to work together as one region and move beyond divisions created by terms such as Polynesia, Melanesia, and Micronesia.

He says while Fiji has taken steps such as increasing the use of solar energy in some island. However, more effort is needed to ensure young people’s voices are heard in climate discussions.

Insert: youths should continue advocating KK 19th Aug

He says the impacts of climate change can already be seen in Fiji, including coastal erosion, rising sea levels, the need for sea walls, and changing cyclone patterns.
